questions.q: Flying only on Aryabhata's planet clock, how far from Mars does his 499 CE Starship arrive?
questions.do: Click the 499 CE Aryabhata card and read Distance off at arrival and the line under it.
questions.a: About 12.1 million km off, roughly 1,789 times the width of Mars. His clock puts Mars about 3.05° from where it really is.

questions.q: Which of the four eras would come closest to Mars, and which clock does it use?
questions.do: Click each era card (499, 550, 628, 640 CE), or read the table All four eras side by side.
questions.a: Nalanda, 640 CE, using Brahmagupta's clock (the newest of the day): Mars error 2.36°, a miss of 9.4 M km, needing a 0.84 km/s fix. Aryabhata's 499 CE mission misses most, by 12.1 M km.

questions.q: How can Aryabhata's ship still reach Mars, and what does the fix cost?
questions.do: Pick the 499 CE Aryabhata card and click Navigator sights Mars mid-cruise. Read the line under Distance off at arrival.
questions.a: Halfway out a navigator sights Mars about 3.0° from where the Aryabhatiya said and burns 1.08 km/s to correct. That costs about 96 t more propellant for a ship carrying 100 t to Mars: one more tanker flight before departure.

questions.q: The old texts track Mars's average motion very well. So why do the clocks still miss Mars by millions of kilometres?
questions.do: Read the paragraph starting Why the clocks miss under the four-era table.
questions.a: Mars's real orbit is noticeably oval, so its true position swings up to about 10° either side of the average. This page flies on the mean motions alone. The siddhantas did have a correction for this (the manda correction), but it is not used here.

questions.q: Which launch date did the Aryabhatiya pick for the Mars trip, and how far is it from the modern model's best date?
questions.do: Click the 499 CE Aryabhata card and read Departure picked by the Aryabhatiya and Modern model's best date.
questions.a: The Aryabhatiya picks 24 Jan 500 CE; the modern model picks 18 Jan 500 CE. That is only 6.6 days apart, more than 1,500 years ago, from a pure count of planet revolutions.
